doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Sessions at Olympic Studios with Clapton and the Stones
summary: Taking the train to London to play sessions, meeting Charlie Watts and Eric Clapton, and the open scene before the record business took over.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I wonder, I’m picturing a scenario that you write home to whomever and, “Yeah studies are going good and yeah, and I’m doing sessions with Eric Clapton and the Rolling Stones.”
I didn’t write that. It was such a smaller scene back then. Like if you say the Rolling Stones now what you picture is a billion dollar organization going around the world in

trucks and planes and stuff. But back, this was 1967, 1968 — I mean they were well known, they had some hit records, but there was a scene — this one particular recording studio, it was called Olympic Studios, it was outside of London. I went to school in Brighton, which was a one hour train ride up to London. And while I was in graduate school friends of mine from San Francisco had come over to England, they had been signed to Capitol Records and they were going to make their first record in England. And so I would go up at night on the train and play on the sessions, hang out with the musicians. And in this studio, Olympic Studios, everybody was just hanging out. I got to know Charlie Watts pretty well, a big jazz fan. Eric Clapton showed up on a session I was doing with an American guitar player named Jesse Ed Davis. I mean people were just hanging out. And there was some advantage to being an American musician who had not just listened to the records but been there and seen it. I mean Peter Frampton and Eric Clapton were both completely obsessed with playing the blues. And when you came and you had spent some time in Chicago and yeah, I saw Muddy Waters or such people. It was very open that way. It wasn’t, you know, very soon thereafter the record business took over the music industry and everything became frankly about money. But, there was that period, and particularly in England I think because the success that the British musicians had in the United States made a lot of musicians in the United States sit up and pay attention to our own music. There was a time when it was all available, and people were hanging out and I don’t think we thought about it or I certainly didn’t think about it as being unusual. It was only years later when somebody would say like, “Well you know what was Mick Jagger like?” Well he was a nice, polite guy. I mean he was just a guy. And the record business really separates musicians based on economics. So when Herbie Hancock for example got really famous back in the early ‘70s, one of the effects of that is it pulled him out of the pool. You weren’t hanging out with Herbie Hancock anymore. Anyway, no I never wrote home about any of it, I just thought it was the way things were.
